unitDescription.value:
In this unit, students develop foundation skills in workshop production, technical drawing and basic electronics through the manufacture of a handheld LED torch. Students interpret an engineering drawing, identify materials and components, and follow a planned production sequence to construct the torch from aluminium and hardboard Masonite.

Students learn about basic DC circuits, including voltage, current, resistance, conductors, insulators, switches, LEDs and batteries. They apply safe workshop practices while marking out, cutting, drilling, countersinking, filing, finishing and assembling their product. Sustainability is explored through the properties and recycling of aluminium, battery disposal and the responsible use of materials. Students test their completed torch and evaluate its function, finish and suitability for its intended user.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: Students at St Brendan’s College operate within a diverse learning environment where practical, hands-on application is essential to engagement and skill acquisition. The Year 7–8 Design Technologies curriculum is structured to accommodate varying levels of prior experience with digital systems and manual production techniques. Learning experiences leverage the College’s commitment to vocational pathways and technical literacy, ensuring that students develop fundamental design-thinking skills alongside an appreciation for safety, sustainability, and material performance. Tasks are designed to build student confidence through scaffolded inquiry and iterative prototyping, providing frequent opportunities for students to connect design solutions to authentic, real-world community contexts. Literacy and numeracy support is integrated across all units, ensuring students can effectively communicate design proposals and analyse project data. Teachers differentiate instruction to support the specific needs of the cohort, fostering resilience and independent problem-solving through reflective practice and iterative design cycles that align with the achievement standards of the Australian Curriculum.

description.value:
Students will manufacture a functional handheld LED torch using the supplied engineering drawing and materials. The torch must contain a working DC circuit consisting of a CR2032 power source, switching mechanism and LED load.

Students will demonstrate their ability to safely select and use workshop tools, accurately measure and mark materials, cut and shape components, drill and countersink holes, finish surfaces and assemble the product. They will also complete a folio and theory activities demonstrating their understanding of technical drawings, electricity, voltage, current, resistance, button battery safety, aluminium recycling and production processes.

At the end of the project, students will test and evaluate the completed torch against the supplied specifications.

They communicate design ideas and solutions to audiences using technical terms and graphical representation techniques, including using digital tools. They independently and collaboratively document and manage production processes to safely produce designed solutions.

theory.value: Explicit instruction focuses on Work Health and Safety (WHS) requirements, specifically the legal and personal responsibilities within a manufacturing setting. Students learn to decode technical communication by studying engineering drawings, identifying various line types—such as visible, hidden, centre, and dimension lines—and understanding the difference between isometric and orthogonal projections. Classroom discussion covers the importance of standard symbols and how they communicate design intent and manufacturing constraints within the industry.

In the practical setting, they practice measuring and marking out on scrap material using steel rules, try squares, and scribers to achieve millimetre precision. The week concludes with students practicing centre punching techniques on aluminium offcuts, focusing on the correct use of the ball-peen hammer to create a physical guide for future drilling tasks.

activities.title: WHS Hierarchy & Legal Responsibilities
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly present and define the core Work Health and Safety vocabulary on the whiteboard. Define WHS as statutory legislation establishing safe working parameters, and Duty of Care as the personal and collective obligation to avoid acts or omissions causing foreseeable harm. Distinguish clearly between a 'Hazard' (an intrinsic condition or item with harm potential) and a 'Risk' (the probability and severity of exposure to that hazard). Model how this applies to St Brendan's College workshop rules (e.g. wearing safety glasses to prevent flying metal swarf). Rear-of-room monitoring during recording.
activities.studentsDo: In the workbook, complete the formal definitions for the 4 core terms: WHS, Duty of Care, Hazard, and Risk.
activities.visibleInstructions: Write complete definitions for each of the 4 statutory safety terms in the workbook table.
activities.questioning:
q: Why is Duty of Care considered a non-negotiable legal obligation rather than a simple workplace suggestion?
Expected: It is written into statutory WHS legislation and holds every individual accountable for preventing foreseeable injury to themselves and others.
q: How does an unguarded bench vise represent both a hazard and a risk?
Expected: The vise itself is the physical hazard because of its heavy steel jaws and pinch points; the risk is the likelihood of a student crushing fingers or striking an elbow if proper clearance protocols are ignored.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
1. WHS: Workplace Health and Safety statutory legislation governing workplace welfare, health, and physical protection.
2. Duty of Care: A legal and moral responsibility requiring every person to take reasonable care for their own safety and the safety of others.
3. Hazard: Any situation, substance, activity, or physical object with the intrinsic potential to cause injury or illness.
4. Risk: The probability, likelihood, and consequence of suffering harm after being exposed to an identified hazard.
activities.eLearning: Project vocabulary definitions on the board. Laptops closed during initial direct instruction.

activities.title: AS 1100 Line Type Vocabulary & Match
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce Australian Standard AS 1100 drafting conventions. Draw each line type on the whiteboard: Visible line (thick, continuous 0.5mm), Hidden line (thin, dashed 0.35mm), Centre line (thin, long-short-long 0.25mm), and Dimension line (thin, continuous with terminal arrowheads). Model an example by writing 'Visible Line' and matching it to its definition, explaining how standard line weights prevent ambiguity in manufacturing and allow fabricators anywhere in Australia to reproduce parts accurately.
activities.studentsDo: Study the board models and complete the line type matching table in the workbook by pairing each AS 1100 line type with its official standard function from the provided definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each AS 1100 line type in column 1 to its correct operational definition by writing the letter of the matching definition from the bank into column 2.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why does AS 1100 specify distinct line thicknesses in addition to line patterns?
Expected: Distinct thicknesses establish visual hierarchy so outlines are instantly recognizable from dimensioning and background detail.
prompt: What does the intersection of two perpendicular centre lines indicate on a drawing?
Expected: It locates the exact centre point of a hole or circular profile for drill alignment.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions in Bank:
A. Thick continuous line (approx 0.5mm) representing physical visible edges and outlines.
B. Thin dashed line (approx 0.35mm) representing concealed edges, internal steps, or hidden geometries.
C. Thin line with arrowheads (approx 0.25mm) defining exact measured distance between points.
D. Thin broken line with alternating long and short dashes (approx 0.25mm) showing axes of symmetry or hole centres.

lessons.title: Marking Out & Centre Punching Precision

activities.title: Demonstration: Datum Edge & Scribing
activities.teacherDoes:
Gather students around the demonstration bench (all wearing safety glasses). Demonstrate inspecting the practice aluminium offcut for a true datum edge. Explicitly show how to align the zero graduation of the steel rule with the datum edge, reading directly from above at 90 degrees to eliminate parallax error. Demonstrate seating the try square stock firmly against the datum edge (showing that any gap leaks light and causes out-of-square lines). Model holding the scriber like a pen angled at 15–20 degrees trailing along the blade in a single smooth pass. Show the contrast between a crisp scribed line and a blunt pencil line on aluminium.

Modelled Example:
'Notice how my thumb firmly presses the try square stock against the reference edge—no daylight visible. When I scribe, I tilt the point at 15 degrees in the direction of travel. I do not press excessively hard; the hardened steel tip cuts a fine, precise V-groove in the aluminium surface.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration at the bench, focusing on the stock placement of the try square and the angle of the scriber. Review the workbook checklist items as they are demonstrated.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher demonstration. Review the Quality Assurance criteria on your workbook checklist before receiving your material.
activities.questioning:
question: What is a datum edge and why must every single measurement originate from it?
expected: A datum edge is a clean, flat reference edge; referencing all marks from one datum prevents cumulative measurement errors.
question: Why is a graphite pencil unsuitable for marking out precision lines on raw aluminium sheet?
expected: Pencil lines are too thick (0.5mm to 1mm wide) for precision fitting and rub off easily during metal handling.
activities.scaffolding:
Core Technique Rules:
1. Datum Edge: The clean reference edge against which tools sit.
2. Parallax Error: The apparent shift in a mark caused by viewing at an angle rather than directly perpendicular.
3. Try Square: Keep stock pressed tight against datum; if light shows through, it is not square.
4. Scriber: Angle at 15 degrees trailing, single firm stroke.

activities.title: Guided Layout & Try Square Alignment
activities.teacherDoes: Issue aluminium offcuts to students at their benches. Guide the class step-by-step: Step 1 - Mark 15mm from the datum edge using the steel rule; call 'Check' and verify 3 student samples aloud. Step 2 - Seat the try square stock against the datum edge, slide to the mark, and visually verify no light shows between stock and aluminium. Step 3 - Scribe a perpendicular line across the face. Step 4 - Measure 15mm along that scribed line to create a crosshair intersection. Circulate through the rows, correcting grip and try square seating.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the step-by-step verbal cadence: measure, align the try square, check for light gaps, and scribe perpendicular intersecting layout lines on their practice aluminium piece.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Measure and mark 15mm from your datum edge.
2. Seat your try square flush against the datum edge.
3. Scribe a sharp 90-degree line across the aluminium.
4. Measure 15mm across to mark the crosshair intersection.
activities.questioning: If you feel the try square rock or wobble as you slide it, what does that indicate? Expected: There is a burr, metal swarf, or deformation on the datum edge that must be filed flat before marking. What happens if you run the scriber back and forth multiple times? Expected: It creates double or ragged lines, making it impossible to identify the true centre when punching.
activities.scaffolding:
Step Sequence:
1. Align steel rule zero flush with datum.
2. Prick mark at 15mm.
3. Place try square stock against datum.
4. Slide blade to prick mark.
5. Scribe once with scriber.
6. Measure 15mm across line to form crosshair (+).

activities.title: Electrical Terminology & Atomic Structure
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly explain atomic structure on the whiteboard, focusing on outer-shell valence electrons. Model how metallic bonding allows outer electrons to dissociate into a delocalised 'sea of electrons', enabling current flow under an electrical potential difference. Why are valence electrons critical to electrical conduction?
Expected: Outer valence electrons are loosely held and can detach to move freely through a metal lattice when voltage is applied.
What makes an electrical insulator atomically different from a conductor?
Expected: Insulators have tightly bound valence electrons that cannot move freely between atoms, blocking charge flow.
activities.scaffolding:
Core definitions:
- Electron: Negatively charged subatomic particle orbiting the nucleus.
- Conductor: Material containing delocalised electrons that permit electric charge to flow freely (e.g. aluminium).
- Insulator: Material with strongly bound electrons that resist electric charge movement (e.g. plastic casing components).

activities.title: Hazard Vocabulary & Biological Impact
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define 'Lithium Coin Cell', 'Electrochemical Burn', and 'Secure Compartment' using clear diagrams on the whiteboard. Explain that when a 3V button battery gets stuck in a wet throat, it creates an electrical current that produces hydroxide (a strong chemical base) which quickly burns through tissue, rather than leaking acid. Delivery script: 'Button batteries like our CR2032 do not need to be leaking to kill or maim. The saliva creates a closed circuit between the positive casing and negative terminal, generating caustic hydroxide that liquefies tissue within two hours.'

activities.questioning: Why is a swallowed button battery more dangerous than a standard cylindrical AA battery? Expected: Its flat coin shape easily lodges in the oesophagus, where saliva bridges the terminals to produce tissue-burning hydroxide ions. What substance is generated by the electrical reaction that causes tissue damage? Expected: Hydroxide ions (caustic soda/alkali), which cause deep liquefaction necrosis rather than battery acid leakage.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Lithium Coin Cell: A small, flat, round 3V battery (e.g. CR2032) used in compact consumer electronic devices.
- Electrochemical Burn: Severe internal tissue necrosis caused when an electric current decomposes moisture/saliva into caustic hydroxide.
- Secure Compartment: A product casing enclosure requiring a specific tool or dual simultaneous hand movements to open.

activities.title: Drilling & Countersink Depth Modeling
activities.teacherDoes: In the workshop, demonstrate how to secure the aluminium workpiece in the drill vice with backing timber to avoid exit blowout. Model aligning the stationary drill bit point into the centre punch indentation. Demonstrate a 'peck-drilling' motion (down-up pulses) to clear aluminium swarf and cool the cutting edge. Swap to a countersink bit and demonstrate depth control—testing repeatedly with an M3 countersunk screw until the screw head sits perfectly flush with the 1.6mm plate surface without cutting through. Delivery script: 'Watch how I peck down lightly twice to clear chips, then pause. For countersinking, one second of light pressure is all it takes—test with your screw before cutting any deeper.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the workshop demonstration closely and complete the pre-start safety checklist in their workbooks, verifying operational rules before beginning work.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher demonstration at the drill press. Note how depth is verified using a physical test screw. Complete your pre-start safety checklist.
activities.questioning: What is the purpose of the 'peck-drilling' motion in aluminium? Expected: It breaks continuous stringy swarf and clears chips, preventing friction heat buildup and tool clogging. What happens if you countersink too deeply into our 1.6mm aluminium plate? Expected: The countersink bit will enlarge the hole completely through the thin plate, ruining structural support for the screw head.
activities.scaffolding:
Key Practical Reminders:
- Align stationary drill point directly in the punch dimple before turning motor on.
- Apply peck drilling: 1 second cut, retract quill slightly to clear swarf, cut again.
- Depth control: Countersink in tiny increments and test fit with an M3 screw after each cut.
- Backing timber: Always support thin plate with timber to prevent burrs and breakthrough grab.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: This week explores the concept of electrical potential through the study of voltage and its role in the torch circuit. In the workshop, students shift from metal to hardboard Masonite, learning the specific handling and cutting requirements for timber-based composites. They focus on creating the internal cavity of the middle plate, which serves as the chassis for the electronic components and determines the spatial layout of the torch.

resources.value: Hardboard Masonite (3mm), coping saws/fret saws, needle files, CR2032 batteries (for sizing), voltage analogy diagrams, steel rules.

theory.value: Students are introduced to voltage using the 'water-pressure' analogy, where voltage is explained as the electrical pressure provided by the CR2032 battery to overcome resistance and light the LED. Instruction covers the specific forward voltage requirements of LEDs and how this must be matched to the 3V power source provided by the lithium cell. Furthermore, students compare the physical properties of Masonite (high-density fibreboard) with aluminium, discussing grain-less structure, moisture sensitivity, and suitability for internal spacers.

prac.value: Students mark out the internal 'pocket' on their Masonite middle plate, using a series of 4mm holes to create an entry point for a coping saw or fret saw. They perform internal piercing cuts to remove the waste material where the battery and switch will sit, demonstrating control over the saw blade to follow complex internal profiles. Edges of the internal cut are then refined using needle files to ensure a snug fit for the CR2032 battery and internal wiring paths.

assessment.value: Formative: Worksheet on voltage and the water-pressure analogy; peer-review of Masonite internal cut quality and dimensional accuracy.

outlineTheme.value: Theory lessons introduce the concept of voltage using the water-pressure analogy to explain the operating requirements of an LED and the power supplied by a CR2032 battery. activities.title: Electrical Potential & Voltage Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define potential difference (voltage), forward voltage drop, and open-circuit battery rating on the whiteboard. Write out the formal definition: 'Voltage is the electrical potential difference or pressure that drives charge through a closed circuit, measured in volts (V).' Explain that white LEDs require a specific forward voltage threshold (typically 2.8V to 3.2V) before any electrons can jump the semiconductor bandgap. Contrast this with the fixed 3.0V chemical potential produced by a standard CR2032 lithium coin cell. Direct students to match the terms to their definitions in the workbook table.

activities.questioning:
Why will a standard white LED stay unlit if supplied with only 1.5 volts from an AA battery? Expected: A single AA battery supplies 1.5V, which is below the 2.8V to 3.2V forward voltage threshold needed to conduct through the LED semiconductor.
What allows our single CR2032 lithium cell to power the LED directly without a step-up converter? Expected: The lithium chemistry delivers a nominal 3.0V, matching the forward voltage rating of the LED.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
1. Voltage (V): The electrical potential difference or pressure that forces free electrons to flow between two points in a circuit.
2. Forward Voltage (Vf): The minimum voltage drop required across an LED semiconductor junction to allow electrical conduction and light emission.
3. CR2032 Nominal Voltage: The 3.0-volt continuous electrical potential supplied by the chemical reaction between lithium and manganese dioxide.

activities.title: Material Properties Audit: Aluminium vs Masonite
activities.teacherDoes: Present raw specimens of 1.6mm aluminium plate and 3.0mm hardboard Masonite under the document camera. Define Masonite as a high-density fibreboard (HDF) manufactured by steam-exploding wood chips and consolidating them under extreme heat and pressure with natural lignin bonding. Contrast its physical and electrical properties directly with aluminium: electrical conductivity (conductor vs insulator), structural grain (both lack natural timber grain/knots), moisture sensitivity (aluminium impervious; Masonite hydroscopic/swells if soaked), and density/shear behaviour. Emphasise that Masonite's insulating property prevents electrical short circuits between the battery terminals and the outer metal casing. Model how to complete the classification audit by evaluating the electrical conductivity of aluminium versus Masonite.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is an electrical insulator essential for the middle plate of our torch?
Expected: Because the positive and negative terminals of the battery and switch sit inside the middle plate; if the middle plate were conductive aluminium, it would create an immediate short circuit.

Expected: It is an engineered composite made from randomised, steam-exploded wood fibres compressed with lignin, giving it uniform density in all directions.
activities.scaffolding:

- Electrical Insulator: Materials with tightly bound valence electrons preventing charge flow (Masonite).
- Moisture Sensitive: Absorbs atmospheric moisture and swells when wet (Masonite).
- High Tensile Strength: Resists stretching and tensile pulling forces without breaking (Aluminium).
- Uniform/Grain-less Structure: Consistent composition across all axes without natural grain lines (Both).

activities.title: Coping Saw Setup & Piercing Cut Demonstration
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the central demonstration bench. Demonstrate drilling the 4mm entry hole in the internal waste area of a Masonite plate using the pedestal drill press, emphasising clamping with a timber backing block to prevent breakout. Move to the woodworking vice: demonstrate how to unhook one end of a coping saw blade, thread the blade through the drilled hole, re-attach it to the frame, and verify that the blade teeth point backwards toward the handle (cutting on the pull stroke). Explain that cutting on the pull stroke keeps the thin sheet flat against the vice support and prevents buckled blades. Demonstrate tensioning the handle and mounting the workpiece with soft jaws. Modelled example: 'Notice how the teeth angle down toward the handle. When I pull back, the blade bites cleanly without lifting the 3mm hardboard.'

q: Why must the teeth of a coping saw point backwards toward the handle when performing internal cuts in thin sheet material?
Expected: Pull-stroke cutting pulls the workpiece down firmly against the vice support, providing greater control and preventing thin 3mm sheet from chattering or snapping the blade.
q: What is the purpose of placing a scrap timber backing block beneath the Masonite during drilling?
Expected: It supports the bottom fibres of the board, preventing breakout or ragged delamination as the drill bit exits.

Setup Checklist Items:
1. Safety glasses donned and long hair tied back.
2. 4mm entry hole drilled with scrap timber backing block.
3. Blade unhooked from top pin and threaded through the entry hole.
4. Blade teeth pointing backward toward the handle (pull-stroke orientation).
5. Frame handle turned clockwise to tension blade firmly without bowing.
6. Masonite clamped securely in vice using timber soft jaws.

lessons.title: Surface Finishing & Deburring Techniques
lessons.learningGoal: apply correct grit sequences and deburring techniques to achieve a professional, safe surface finish on machined plates

orientate.smartStart: Examine the cut aluminium plate on your bench. In your workbook, list 3 distinct workshop hazards caused by un-deburred metal edges and drill burrs (e.g., lacerations to hands, stripped wire insulation, uneven plate seating during assembly).

activities.title: I Do: Deburring & Sanding Sequence Demonstration
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the demonstration bench. Model the safe grip and rotational motion of a handheld swivel deburring tool along a drilled 3mm hole in aluminium plate. Contrast with using a fine smooth file held at 45 degrees along the straight edges. Demonstrate progressive sanding: start with 120-grit dry paper on a flat block to remove hacksaw gouges, progress to 240-grit dry to smooth scratches, and conclude with 400-grit wet paper lubricated with water for a uniform brushed satin finish. Emphasise keeping strokes parallel to the long edge to establish a clean grain. Modelled example: 'Notice how I wrap the abrasive paper tightly over the timber block rather than folding it over my fingertips; using a flat backing prevents rounding off the sharp 90-degree corners of our torch plate.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration at the workbench. Follow along with the safety and procedural sequence, ticking each item on the procedural checklist in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher demonstration. Verify each workshop safety rule and procedural step by checking the boxes on your workbook checklist.
activities.questioning:
What visual evidence indicates that a technician is ready to switch from 120-grit to 240-grit sandpaper?
Expected: When all deep hacksaw and file scratches have been replaced by a consistent, uniform pattern of fine 120-grit scratches.
Why do we apply water when sanding metal with 400-grit wet-and-dry paper?
Expected: The water acts as a lubricant to flush away aluminium swarf and prevent the paper pores from clogging (loading), ensuring a smooth satin finish.
activities.scaffolding: Finishing rules: 1. Always mount paper onto a wooden sanding block to maintain plate flatness. 2. Sand in a single direction parallel to the longest datum edge. 3. Grit progression order: 120 (coarse/dry) -> 240 (medium/dry) -> 400 (fine/wet).
activities.transition: Now that you have verified the safety and setup steps, let us sequence the precise workflow before you handle tools at your bench vices.

activities.title: I Do: Modeling the Dry-Fit Assembly
activities.teacherDoes: Model the dry-fit assembly at the central bench: stack bottom aluminium plate, Masonite spacer core, and top aluminium plate. Insert four temporary M3 alignment machine screws through corner holes. Explain how to test for hole concentricity (screws must drop through by hand without binding or cross-threading). Demonstrate how to test external perimeter flushness by running a fingernail across seams to detect stepped overhangs. Test-fit a dummy slide switch into the internal cutout to verify depth and travel clearance. Model ticking the demonstration verification checklist in the workbook. For example, state: 'Notice how the M3 screw drops freely through the top plate, spacer, and base without resistance; if it binds, our pilot hole centres are misaligned.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's dry-fit procedure at the central workbench. Follow each diagnostic check and complete the alignment verification checklist in your workbook as each step is demonstrated.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher demonstrate the dry-fit assembly. Verify each structural alignment check by ticking the corresponding box in your workbook checklist.

q: If an M3 alignment screw cannot pass through all three plates without binding, what manufacturing fault has occurred?
expected: The corner mounting holes across the plates are non-concentric (misaligned hole centres).
q: Why must we conduct a dry-fit before wiring and soldering circuit components?
expected: Filing, drilling, or adjusting plate profiles after mounting electronic components creates metal swarf that causes short circuits and damages components.

activities.title: Electrical Resistance Vocabulary & Concepts
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly introduce 'Resistance' as the opposition to the flow of electric charge, measured in Ohms (Ω). activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Resistance: The opposition to the flow of electric current through a conductor or component.
- Ohm (Ω): The SI unit of measurement for electrical resistance.
- Current Limiting: Restricting current magnitude to protect components from thermal and electrical overload.

activities.teacherDoes: Deliver explicit instruction on the three primary physical variables determining conductor resistance: material resistivity, conductor length, and cross-sectional area. q: How does increasing conductor length affect the total resistance encountered by a moving charge?
expected: Longer distance means electrons must navigate a greater lattice length, accumulating more collisions and higher resistance.
activities.scaffolding:
Conductor Properties Summary:
- Thickness (Cross-sectional Area): Thinner wire = higher resistance; thicker wire = lower resistance.
- Length: Longer conductor = higher resistance; shorter conductor = lower resistance.
- Material: Copper/aluminium = high conductivity; nichrome/insulators = high resistivity.

workbookSpec.title: Technical Analysis: LED Circuit Protection
workbookSpec.prompt: Explain the technical rationale for incorporating current limiting when powering a 5mm LED from a 3V power source.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:

3. Consequence for Longevity: Limiting current protects the LED from overheating, preventing permanent burnout and ensuring reliable operation.

Expected: No, because an LED is a semiconductor diode that blocks reverse current, functioning like an open switch.

activities.teacherDoes:
Demonstrate the step-by-step layout of electrical components inside the CNC-cut or pierced Masonite middle plate under the document camera. Show how to seat the LED flush within the bulb pocket, route insulated wires through internal channels, position the copper switch contact strip, and secure the battery terminal. Explicitly warn students that allowing bare wires or uninsulated leads to contact outer aluminium plates will cause a direct short circuit. Walk through the Pre-Assembly Routing Checklist.

Modelled Example:
'Notice how I trim the positive lead of the LED to length and slip a piece of heat-shrink tubing over the joint before soldering it to the wire. If this bare joint touched the conductive aluminium side plates during the sandwiching process, it would bypass the LED completely and drain the CR2032 cell instantly.'

Expected: It physically separates the conductive contact strip from the battery terminal, creating an open circuit.

activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the life cycle of industrial aluminium, distinguishing between primary production (open-cut bauxite mining, Bayer refining into alumina, Hall-Héroult electrolytic smelting) and secondary production (collection, sorting, and remelting of aluminium scrap). activities.questioning:
q: Why does an LED require a specific orientation in the circuit whereas a resistor does not?
Expected: An LED is a semiconductor diode with polarity (anode and cathode) that only allows current to flow in one direction under forward bias, whereas a resistor restricts current flow equally in either direction.

Definitions for reference:
- Voltage: The electrical pressure or potential difference that drives charge through a circuit (measured in Volts).
- Current: The rate of flow of electrical charge carriers, specifically electrons (measured in Amperes).
- Resistance: The opposition to the flow of electrical current within a conducting path (measured in Ohms).
- Polarity: The directional orientation of a component having positive and negative terminals.
- Insulator: A material with tightly bound valence electrons that blocks the flow of electrical current.

activities.title: Modelled Surface Finishing & Deburring Verification
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher demonstrates the correct sequence of progressive abrasive finishing on a sample aluminium plate, working from 400 through 800 to 1200 grit wet-and-dry paper with a backing block, followed by metal polish. The teacher demonstrates deburring edges with a fine needle file and checking smooth tactile transitions. The teacher emphasizes workshop safety protocols including wearing safety glasses and clamping workpieces using soft-jaw vice guards.
activities.studentsDo: Students observe the teacher's demonstration of progressive grit technique, vice safety, and tactile inspection, then review the quality criteria on their checklist in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the demonstration of surface finishing techniques. Review the checklist items in your workbook to understand the quality standards required for your torch body.
activities.questioning:
prompt: What occurs if an operator skips intermediate grit sizes when progressing from file finishing to metal polish?
expected: Coarse scratches from the file will remain trapped beneath the polish, producing a cloudy and uneven finish rather than a uniform lustre.
prompt: Why must soft jaws or vice guards always be fitted before clamping the aluminium plates in a bench vice?
expected: Soft jaws protect the soft aluminium from being permanently dented or serrated by the hardened steel jaws of the vice.
activities.scaffolding:
Surface finishing sequence:
1. Check all outer edges for burrs using a smooth needle file held flat.
2. Sand along a single direction using 400 grit wet-and-dry paper.
3. Transition to 800 grit, then 1200 grit paper to eliminate micro-scratches.
4. Apply a pea-sized drop of metal polish with a clean cotton rag and buff to a consistent shine.
activities.eLearning: Confirm all students have PPE fitted (safety glasses on, long hair tied back) before any abrasive or polishing work begins.
activities.transition: We will now transition to pairing up to perform a systematic verification of our structural fasteners and switch mechanisms.

workbookSpec.title: Surface Finishing Quality Standards Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify that your aluminium torch components meet all physical quality assurance criteria prior to final assessment.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All four items must be verified and checked off as compliant by the student and subsequently confirmed by the teacher during final moderation.
items: Edges are deburred and smooth to touch with no sharp corners.
Top surface is polished with consistent grit direction and no deep scratches.
No visible scuff marks or indentations from the bench vice jaws.
Screws are countersunk flush with the top plate surface.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All checklist items must be ticked off by the student prior to final teacher grading and moderation against the QCAA achievement standard.

activities.title: Guided Alignment & Switch Integrity Testing
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher guides the class through a systematic structural audit. The teacher demonstrates how to check sandwich plate alignment against datum edges, inspect the perimeter for gaps larger than 0.5 mm, and diagnose switch binding. Modelled instruction: 'If the switch slider binds against the aluminium casing, do not force it. Loosen the retaining screws half a turn, align the parallel edges using an engineer's square, and retighten fasteners in a criss-cross pattern.'
activities.studentsDo: Students work in pairs to audit each other's torches against the four inspection points in the table, recording pass/fail status and noting required physical adjustments.
activities.visibleInstructions: Working with your partner, inspect your torch against each checkpoint in the table. Record Pass or Fail and describe any corrective mechanical action taken.
activities.questioning: If a sliding switch binds or feels stiff during operation, what mechanical adjustment should be attempted first? Expected: Loosen the switch retaining screws slightly, check for trapped metal burrs or Masonite dust in the channel, align the plates squarely, and retighten evenly. What does a visible gap between the Masonite core plate and the outer aluminium plates indicate? Expected: It indicates uneven screw tensioning or residual internal burrs holding the sandwich layers apart.
activities.scaffolding:
Audit checkpoints:
- Masonite core to aluminium plate offset: must be < 0.5 mm
- Switch slide: smooth travel between open and closed positions without jamming
- Fastener tension: all screws tightened uniformly without stripping threads
- Housing gap: zero visible daylight between stacked plates
activities.eLearning: Move between workshop benches to assist student pairs with stiff switch mechanisms or uneven plate clamping.
activities.transition: Now that alignments have been tested and documented, you will proceed to your benches for independent finishing and final assembly adjustments.

workbookSpec.title: Torch Alignment & Switch Diagnostic Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate your assembled LED torch against the following quality assurance checkpoints in pairs.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Inspection Point 1: Pass - Edge flush within 0.5 mm. Inspection Point 2: Fail - De-burred slider slot and re-tensioned screw. Inspection Point 3: Pass - All screws torqued evenly. Inspection Point 4: Pass - Sandwich interfaces flush.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Students must evaluate all 4 inspection points. Correct entries record Pass or Fail status and concrete actions: edge alignment (file/realign), switch slide (deburr/re-tension), fastener torque (tighten in criss-cross pattern), housing gap (clear internal debris).

activities.questioning:
q: How does achieving a uniform surface polish and deburred edges improve the commercial viability of a consumer handheld torch?
Expected: Smooth, deburred finishes eliminate sharp pinch points for the user, improve corrosion resistance, and meet professional aesthetic standards expected in retail products.
q: Why is rubbing in a single uniform direction preferred over circular sanding on flat aluminium plate?
Expected: Unidirectional sanding aligns the micro-scratches along one axis, allowing finer grits and polish to buff them out cleanly without creating swirling scratches.

- 3–4: Edges deburred, surfaces sanded uniformly, minor scratches visible under direct light
- 5: Mirror-like polish, seamless plate alignment, completely flush countersunk fasteners

activities.title: Manufacturing & Material Property Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher defines key engineering terms on the board: Primary Aluminium, Secondary Aluminium, Countersink, Datum Edge, and Malleability. The teacher highlights the distinction between electrolytic bauxite smelting and scrap remelting, and explains why a datum edge is fundamental to layout accuracy. The teacher models matching term 1 to definition E.
activities.studentsDo: Students complete the term-to-definition matching table in their workbooks, entering the corresponding letter from the bank into the Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each material science and manufacturing term on the left with its correct engineering definition from the bank. Write the corresponding letter (A–E) in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does secondary aluminium recycling require 95% less energy than primary extraction from bauxite?
expected: Secondary recycling only requires melting scrap aluminium at approximately 660°C, whereas primary extraction requires huge amounts of electrical energy to break strong aluminium-oxygen bonds in the Hall-Héroult electrolytic process.
question: How does the internal structure of Masonite differ from aluminium when subjected to mechanical drilling?
expected: Masonite is an engineered composite of compressed wood fibres that can fray or tear if drilled without backing support, whereas aluminium is a ductile metal that yields clean, sheared chips.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Primary Aluminium: Metal extracted directly from raw bauxite ore via energy-intensive electrolytic smelting.
- Secondary Aluminium: Recycled metal produced by melting existing scrap, requiring approximately 5% of primary extraction energy.
- Countersink: A conical enlargement cut into the mouth of a hole to allow a countersunk screw head to sit flush with the surface.
- Datum Edge: A true, flat reference edge from which all layout markings and dimensions are measured to prevent cumulative error.
- Malleability: The property of a metal that allows it to be hammered, rolled, or deformed under compressive stress without fracturing.
activities.eLearning: Students focus entirely on workbook completion and board explanations.
activities.transition: We will now use our understanding of metal properties and tolerances to reconstruct the complete assembly flow of the LED torch.

activities.title: Manufacturing Step Sequence & Tool Selection
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher reviews the chronological manufacturing process for the LED torch from raw stock to finished assembly. The teacher models chronological reasoning: 'We cannot drill holes before scribing layout lines from our datum edge, and we never polish before machining because files and drill swarf would ruin the polished face.' The teacher guides students through ordering the five operations.
activities.studentsDo: Students order the scrambled bank of manufacturing operations into the five blank chronological slots in their workbooks.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the bank of workshop operations. Place each operation in its correct chronological order from step 1 (earliest) to step 5 (final) in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
q: Why must centre punching always precede drilling in metal fabrication?
Expected: The conical indentation from the centre punch seats the drill bit chisel edge, preventing the bit from wandering across the work surface.
q: Why is establishing a true datum edge critical before any scribing occurs?
Expected: Scribing from a common true datum edge ensures all dimensions relate to a single reference, preventing additive measurement errors across the plate.
activities.scaffolding:
Chronological sequence rules:
- Stage 1: Surface prep and layout referencing (datum edge, scriber, rule)
- Stage 2: Material severance (hacksaw cutting)
- Stage 3: Hole placement and machining (centre punch, drill press, countersink)
- Stage 4: Edge and face refinement (needle files, deburring)
- Stage 5: Final surface finishing and assembly (abrasive progression, polish, fasteners)

activities.title: Modelled Quality Control Inspection
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the precise use of vernier callipers to measure outer dimensions against the 120.0mm (+/- 1.0mm) drawing tolerance. Demonstrate how to check switch actuation continuity and feel, and how to inspect plate sandwich alignment under directional workbench lighting. Explicitly point out non-conformance defects such as protruding screw heads or plate overhang. activities.questioning:
Why do manufacturing drawings state a tolerance range (e.g., +/- 1.0mm) rather than a single fixed dimension?
Expected: Because no manufacturing process is perfectly exact; tolerances define the acceptable limits where parts will still fit and function correctly.
What is the structural consequence if the countersink hole is drilled too shallow on the aluminium top plate?
Expected: The fastener head will sit proud of the surface, catching on hands or pockets and preventing flush stacking.

Quality Criteria Thresholds:
- Overall Length: 120.0 mm (+/- 1.0 mm)

activities.teacherDoes: Supervise practical corrective work at the benches. activities.questioning:
question: Why must polishing paste be buffed completely dry rather than left in component crevices?
expected: Residual paste can cause chemical tarnishing over time and foul electrical contacts if it migrates into the internal switch cavity.
question: How does cross-tensioning opposite screws maintain equal pressure across the Masonite core?
expected: It prevents the plates from warping or bowing, ensuring uniform clamping on the battery terminals.
activities.scaffolding:
Rectification Tools & Techniques:
- Edge burrs: Use a fine needle file at 45 degrees along the perimeter.
- Surface scratches: Rub in parallel strokes using 400-grit wet/dry abrasive, followed by polishing compound.
- Fastener tension: Tighten diagonally across the plate to distribute clamping pressure.

activities.title: Technical Evaluative Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach how to write high-level evaluative responses using QCAA design terminology. Contrast weak statements ('The torch looks nice') with technical evaluation statements ('The high strength-to-weight ratio of 6060 aluminium provides structural rigidity while maintaining ergonomic portability for night inspections'). Guide students through the technical vocabulary cloze task, modelling how to read surrounding context clues in the sentence to select the correct engineering term.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze exercise in the workbook by selecting technical terms from the word bank that describe manufacturing precision and user suitability.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the word bank to complete the technical evaluative sentences in your workbook. Ensure every term is placed in its correct engineering context.
activities.questioning:
Why is the term 'dimensional tolerance' more objective than 'good size' when evaluating a manufactured product?
Expected: 'Dimensional tolerance' refers to quantifiable, measurable variance from an engineering drawing rather than subjective opinion.
What does 'ergonomic efficiency' mean in relation to the torch switch design?
Expected: It means the switch is positioned and shaped so the user can easily activate it single-handedly with their thumb without strain.
activities.scaffolding:
Evaluation Terminology:
- Dimensional tolerance: Permissible variation from specified drawing dimensions.
- Dielectric insulation: Non-conductive property preventing unwanted electrical short circuits.
- Ergonomic efficiency: Physical design optimised for human hand comfort and intuitive operation.
- Structural integrity: Ability to withstand applied mechanical forces and drop impacts without failure.

activities.questioning:
q: What trade-off occurs if we switch from screw fasteners to permanent blind rivets?
Expected: Assembly speed increases and screws cannot vibrate loose, but the product can no longer be disassembled for battery replacement or maintenance.

Expected: It eliminates manual bending errors, reduces internal resistance, and prevents contacts from loosening over time.
